name: Yara Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Yara, and thank you for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say out loud and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I run a blasthole drill at the Kestrel iron ore pit. The drill makes the holes in the rock where the explosives go, in a neat pattern the engineers design. My rig already does a lot by itself, it finds the hole position by GPS and it drills the depth automatically, so my job is half watching and half fixing what it gets wrong. I'm three years in. Before that I ran a family daycare from my house for nineteen years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's quite a change. What do you like and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love learning it. I ask an AI chat tool about everything, why the bit is wearing unevenly, what a fault code means, and then I check it with Ruth, my trainer, who's been drilling for twenty years. The hard part is being slow in front of twenty-five-year-olds, and the noise, even with the ear muffs. My husband Samir is a high school maths teacher and he jokes that I'm the only grandmother in the country who reads drill manuals for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? That'd be a bit of a let-down, if I'm honest. I've seen what the tools can do already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overblown but the tools are still useful, and I'd keep using them. I'd probably post that it's a good thing we didn't let a few companies remake the whole economy overnight. Slow is fine if it's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means a quiet finish to my working life. I'd get maybe six more years drilling, I'd get better at it, and the pay would keep going into savings. Part of me would miss the excitement, though, which is a strange thing to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, asking the AI about faults and practising patterns on the training simulator. I'd sign up for the next level of drill ticket, that's the certificate, in the new year. And I'd keep putting a third of my pay away, like Samir and I agreed when I took the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit disappointed, like a film that was supposed to have a big ending and just stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said slow is fine if it's fair. Fair to who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To the people who do the work. I ran a daycare, I know how often the people doing the hard, careful stuff get paid the least. If AI had come in fast and only the owners got richer, I'd be angry. So a slow, boring version isn't the worst thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ruth use the AI tools like you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she thinks I'm mad. She says the rock will tell you what it's doing if you listen. And she's right half the time. I like having both, her ears and the chatbot.

S0.say: The hype was overblown but the tools are still useful, and it's good that a few companies didn't remake the economy overnight. Slow is fine if it's fair.
S0.think: It means a quiet finish to her working life, with six more years of drilling and saving. Part of her would miss the excitement.
S0.do: Keeps using AI to diagnose faults and practising on the simulator. Signs up for the next drill certificate in the new year and keeps saving a third of her pay.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small disappointment, like a film that stopped before its big ending.
S0.quote: I like having both, her ears and the chatbot.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is unusual: a late entrant who is excited by the technology that threatens her job. Her daycare years shape her sense of fairness towards careful, low-paid work. She admits she'd find the slow version a bit boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I believe. I'm already living the start of it on my rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains have to be shared, through better pay, shorter weeks, or public money for retraining. Mining companies are making a fortune off fewer workers, so they can pay for it. I'd say it at the union meeting and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. The company is going to need people to run drills from the remote operations centre in the city, and I'd be one of the first to put my hand up. My age matters less there, it's screens and patience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the remote operations training the moment it's advertised, this year if I could. I'd keep a notebook of every fault the auto-drill makes, because that's exactly what the remote team will need to know. And I'd help Ruth with the screens if she wanted, so she doesn't get pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited. I'd worry for the older drillers, but not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The remote centre is in the city. Would you move or drive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wouldn't move, the grandkids are here. It's fly-in fly-out for some people, or a long drive. I'd do a week-on, week-off roster if I had to, the kids are grown and Samir has his school. Honestly, a week in the city might be fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd help Ruth. Would she let you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first, she's proud. But I'd make it a swap, I teach her the screens, she teaches me to hear the rock. That's how it worked in daycare too, the older mums taught me things and I helped them with the online bookings.

S1.say: The gains have to be shared through better pay, shorter weeks or public retraining money, paid for by mining companies making a fortune off fewer workers.
S1.think: She'd be fine, maybe better than fine, because the company will need people at the remote operations centre and she'd volunteer first. Her age matters less there.
S1.do: Applies for remote operations training the moment it's advertised and keeps a notebook of every fault the auto-drill makes. Offers to help her trainer with the screens so she isn't pushed out.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a bit excited, with worry for older drillers.
S1.quote: I teach her the screens, she teaches me to hear the rock.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as an opening, not a threat, and plans to move early. Her politics stay firmly about sharing gains even though she personally expects to do well. She thinks immediately about protecting a colleague who is less comfortable with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Two years. That's not something you can learn your way through, is it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments must step in immediately, with a public income for people who lose work and a tax on the companies that profit. I'd be loud about it, at the union and online, and I'd go to rallies. This is the moment we either share it or we don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, honestly, I'd be okay. I've got savings, Samir's salary, the house is paid off, and I'm close to retiring anyway. What scares me is the town. Half the people I know drive trucks or work the processing plant, and they'd all be out at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting money into extra savings and start using it to help, maybe pay for my nephew's rent for a while if he loses his job. I'd volunteer with the union on a plan for a public jobs scheme. I'd keep using every AI tool I can, because if I understand them, I can explain them to people who are frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for myself so much, more like watching a storm come towards your neighbours' houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only 2 years take away, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it properly. With two years, you can't build a retraining scheme, you can't set up a fair tax, the robots are just there. I'd have no time to get into the remote centre either, because it would be robots running robots. With more time, people like me can be a bridge. With two years there's no bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be okay. Is that the whole truth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I'd lose the last few years of good pay and I'd miss the work, I really would. But I'm not going to pretend I'm suffering when Samir's still teaching and we own the house. Maybe his job goes too, though, AI teachers. I hadn't thought of that until now.

S2.say: Governments must step in at once with a public income for people who lose work and a tax on the companies that profit. She'd be loud at the union, online and at rallies.
S2.think: She'd personally be okay with savings, a paid-off house and her husband's salary. What scares her is the whole town losing work at once.
S2.do: Stops building extra savings and uses the money to help family, such as her nephew's rent. Volunteers on a union plan for a public jobs scheme and keeps using AI tools so she can explain them to frightened neighbours.
S2.feel: Uneasy, like watching a storm head for her neighbours' houses.
S2.quote: With more time, people like me can be a bridge. With two years there's no bridge.
S2.fieldNote: Her own position is secure, so her unease is mostly for her community. Asked to be honest, she admitted she'd miss the work and then realised mid-answer that her husband's teaching job might also be at risk. Her adaptability can't help much when the timeline leaves no gap to adapt into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a different feeling. That's enough for me to finish the job and hand over well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up something fair if governments start now. Training money, early pensions for older workers, and a share of the profits going back to mining towns. I'd keep saying it until someone listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it lines up almost perfectly. I'd move into the remote centre in the first year or two, work there until I'm sixty-two or sixty-three, and retire as the robots take over. I'd feel lucky, and a bit guilty about feeling lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the remote centre in the first year and push the company to train older drillers too, not just young ones. I'd help set up a little study group at the union hall for people who want to learn AI tools, maybe Tuesday nights. And I'd start talking with Samir about where we want to be in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of guilt underneath. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the 2-year picture you said there was no bridge. What does the bridge look like with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like people like me teaching people like Ruth, and Ruth teaching the young ones what the rock does. It looks like the company paying for courses while people still have pay coming in. Five years is enough for one round of that. Ten would be enough for two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I came into mining late, for the money, and I'd get out clean. Ruth gave her whole life to it and she'd be the one struggling. That doesn't feel right. I can't fix it, but I can try to help her through it.

S3.say: Five years is enough to set up something fair if governments start now, with training money, early pensions and profits going back to mining towns.
S3.think: The timing lines up almost perfectly: remote centre for a few years, then retirement as robots take over. She'd feel lucky and a bit guilty about it.
S3.do: Applies to the remote centre in the first year and pushes the company to train older drillers too. Starts a Tuesday-night AI study group at the union hall and plans the next five years with Samir.
S3.feel: Mostly calm and hopeful, with some guilt underneath.
S3.quote: I came into mining late, for the money, and I'd get out clean. Ruth gave her whole life to it and she'd be the one struggling.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year warning lets her play the bridge role she wants, and she clearly enjoys teaching. Her guilt about getting out cleanly compared with her lifelong-miner trainer is the most personal moment of the interview. Her politics and her plans point the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'll be retired by then, sitting on the porch reading about it on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to do the transition properly, with real planning and real money behind it. Mining towns have been through booms and busts before, we know what happens without a plan. I'd say it at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's barely a problem. I'll work six more years, maybe in the remote centre, and retire before 2036. My worry is for my grandkids, and for whether the country is fair enough to share what the robots make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, move to the remote centre if it opens, and keep saving. I'd stay active in the union and vote for parties that want a share of AI profits to go to everyone. I'd help my daughter think about what my grandkids should study, maybe something with people, like nursing or teaching, though I don't really know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even, if we do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is there anything you'd start now that you wouldn't in the faster ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a little project, maybe teaching older people in town how to use the AI tools, at the library. With two years, it'd be crisis mode. With ten, you can actually teach, slowly, the way people learn best. That's my daycare brain talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't really know what the grandkids should study. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I always had an answer for parents at daycare, which school, which teacher. Now I don't. But I'd rather say I don't know than pretend.

S4.say: This is the chance to plan the transition properly with real money behind it, because mining towns know what happens without a plan.
S4.think: It's barely a problem for her because she'll retire before 2036. Her worry is her grandchildren and whether the country shares what robots make.
S4.do: Keeps working, moves to the remote centre if it opens and keeps saving. Stays active in the union, votes for parties that want AI profits shared and helps her daughter think about the grandchildren's studies.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, if it's done right.
S4.quote: With ten, you can actually teach, slowly, the way people learn best. That's my daycare brain talking.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade of warning Yara starts planning community projects, like teaching older people AI tools at the library. Her daycare background keeps coming back as a way she understands learning. She is honest that she doesn't know what to advise her grandchildren.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, but for the town, not for me. Everyone losing work at the same time, with no plan, that's how places like ours fall apart. What would help is a public income for people who lose work, paid for by the companies, and money for towns like ours to build something new.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. Mining was mostly men for a long time, and some of us came in late because the money was finally open to us. It'd be a shame if the door closed just as we got through it.

headlineQuote: It'd be a shame if the door closed just as we got through it.
portrait: Yara Usman is a 58-year-old blasthole drill operator at an iron ore pit who ran a home daycare for nineteen years before starting in mining three years ago. She uses AI tools every day to learn her rig and loves the technology, while staying firmly progressive about sharing its gains through unions and public money. With savings, a paid-off house and her husband's teaching salary, she stays calm in most pictures and plans to move into remote operations early. Even the two-year AGI picture makes her only uneasy, mostly for her town and her colleagues, though she noticed mid-interview that her husband's job might also be at risk.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because everyone in her town would lose work at once with no plan, which is how places like hers fall apart.
whatWouldHelp: A public income for people who lose work, paid for by the companies, and money for mining towns to build something new.
